headlines.article_text: Amazon faces FAA probe after delivery drone strikes Michigan garage Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The FAA said it will investigate an Amazon drone crash near Detroit, Michigan. An Amazon spokesperson told CNBC there were no injuries and the drone has been removed. Amazon has been working to make drone delivery a reality for nearly 13 years. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon's new MK30 Prime Air drone is displayed during Amazon's "Delivering the Future" event at the company's BFI1 Fulfillment Center, Robotics Research and Development Hub in Sumner, Washington on Oct. 18, 2023. Jason Redmond | AFP | Getty Images The Federal Aviation Administration said Monday it will investigate a recent Amazon drone crash near Detroit. On Friday, one of Amazon's MK30 drones "landed on a resident's garage" during a delivery in Huntington Woods, Michigan, a suburb north of Detroit, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner told CNBC in a statement. The crash occurred after the drone dropped off a customer's shampoo order around 4:30 p.m. local time, and one of its propellers was damaged in the incident, according to ABC affiliate WXYZ . A preliminary incident report posted to the FAA's website states the drone "struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." The report says the condition of the drone is unknown. Stelzner said there were no injuries, the drone has been removed and Amazon is in contact with the resident. "Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare," Stelzner said. "Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service." An FAA spokesperson confirmed it's investigating the incident. A spokesperson for the National Transportation Safety Board, a federal agency that also investigates aviation accidents, said it's aware of the incident and is continuing to gather information. The agency hasn't yet determined whether it will open a probe, the NTSB spokesperson added. Amazon has been working to make widespread drone delivery a reality ever since founder Jeff Bezos laid out his vision for the program nearly 13 years ago. The rollout has been slow, as the program encountered regulatory delays and staff cuts , as well as technical challenges and pushback from some communities where it conducted early pilots. Expansion has recently ramped up. The company is targeting a launch of its drone service in 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year, while an Amazon executive claimed it has the "highest demand drone delivery service in the industry," CNBC previously reported . The e-commerce giant has encountered some challenges along the way. Federal investigators opened a probe nearly one year ago after an Amazon drone downed an internet cable in Waco, Texas. One month earlier, a separate federal probe was opened into an incident near Phoenix, where two Amazon drones collided with a construction crane. headlines.article_text: CrowdStrike CEO defends $44 billion Zscaler deal Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz defended the company's $44 billion acquisition of Zscaler, calling the deal a "winning combination." Kurtz said the acquisition will strengthen CrowdStrike's network security capabilities and create significant cross-selling opportunities while delivering immediate financial benefits. In this article CRWD ZS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:36 01:36 CrowdStrike CEO on deal to buy Zscaler Mad Money with Jim Cramer CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz on Monday defended the cybersecurity company's planned acquisition of Zscaler , arguing the deal will strengthen its security capabilities and create significant growth opportunities despite a sharp sell-off in its shares. "When you look at the tailwinds from these agentic attacks and you listen to customers, they're looking for a complete solution and a platform that delivers not only all of the capabilities we have, but also has network visibility, protection, and control, and zero trust from a network perspective," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on " Mad Money ." "This is why we acquired Zscaler today. The technology, the team, and we think it's a winning combination putting it together with the CrowdStrike platform." Shares of CrowdStrike fell roughly 9% Monday after the company announced it would acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $44 billion, raising investor concerns about dilution. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. Zscaler shares rose more than 17%. The acquisition overshadowed CrowdStrike's better-than-expected quarterly results released Monday morning. The company had been scheduled to report earnings on Dec. 1, but moved up the release date to coincide with the Zscaler announcement. The acquisition fills a key gap in CrowdStrike's cybersecurity platform. While its Falcon platform protects devices and cloud systems, Zscaler adds security across the networks connecting them. Kurtz said the deal expands CrowdStrike's addressable market by roughly $185 billion. CrowdStrike's largest acquisition to date comes amid a wave of consolidation in the cybersecurity industry as companies ramp up defenses against increasingly sophisticated AI-powered attacks. Recent high-profile hacks and technology outages have heightened concerns about vulnerabilities in corporate systems. CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares having soared about 96% this year entering Monday's session. For its part, Zscaler's stock ended last week down 13% year to date. As of Friday's close, the companies had a combined market value of more than $265 billion, trailing industry leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion. Kurtz also highlighted the potential to sell more products across the combined customer base. He said the companies share only about 2,000 accounts, leaving roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not currently use CrowdStrike. The companies are "very complementary overall," Kurtz said. "There's very little overlap." He emphasized that the announcement generated an overwhelmingly positive response from customers. "Most important, customers demanded it. They loved it, and I can tell you, my phone blew up after the acquisition," Kurtz said. "There's so many customers that love both us and Zscaler, and they're excited to see the acquisition news today." To be sure, the all-stock deal has raised concerns about dilution, since CrowdStrike will issue new shares to pay for the acquisition, reducing existing shareholders' ownership stakes. Kurtz pushed back on those concerns, arguing that the combination will deliver immediate financial benefits. "On a free cash flow per share basis, it's immediately accretive right after close," he said. "With just modest synergies, you're going to have revenue, operating margin, and free cash flow margin accretion." He also downplayed integration risks, pointing to the companies' longstanding technology partnership. That relationship dates back to at least 2019 , and the firms announced an expanded partnership in August 2025 . "Zscaler is our No. 1 technology partner," Kurtz said. In a separate "Mad Money" interview, Zscaler CEO and Founder Jay Chaudhry emphasized that combining the companies' platforms will better position them to combat a new generation of AI-powered cyberattacks. "I think there's some areas where, by bringing the platforms together, we can become the best protection against AI attacks. headlines.article_text: AI adoption grows in Asia, but measuring the gains remains tricky Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had surpassed initial costs, according to an AWS survey. More businesses are moving AI projects from experimentation into production, AWS executive Jaime Vallés told CNBC. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of businesses, according to the survey. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon Web Services AI data center in New Carlisle, Indiana, on Oct. 2, 2025. Noah Berger | Getty Images Businesses across Asia-Pacific say their investments in artificial intelligence are paying off, with the technology helping boost productivity and revenue. But putting a number on those gains is proving far less straightforward. Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had already surpassed their initial costs, yet just 12% were very confident in their ability to accurately measure their return on investment, according to research conducted by Strand Partners for Amazon Web Services . APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation. Jaime Vallés VP, Amazon Web Services The survey included 9,750 business leaders across 10 Asia-Pacific markets: Australia, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The biggest shift over the past year has been the growing number of companies moving AI projects into production, Jaime Vallés, AWS vice president for Asia Pacific, Japan and China, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "From year over year, probably the biggest difference is you're seeing a lot of ideas put into production," Vallés said. From pilots to results Despite the reported financial benefits, many businesses remain in the early stages of AI adoption. The survey found that 64% of businesses using AI across Asia-Pacific and Japan still rely on general-purpose AI tools or ready-made solutions for specific tasks, while only 19% of businesses have a formal and comprehensive AI strategy. Among those with such an AI strategy, 35% had reached the most advanced stage of adoption, compared with just 8% of businesses without one, according to the research. Technology alone is not enough to turn AI investments into meaningful business outcomes, Vallés said. He pointed to what he called the "four Rs of readiness": technological, cultural, skills and personal readiness. "Where we see more meaningful impact is when you see the leadership using AI, building a culture of using AI and using AI to transform and not automate," Vallés said. Financial services is among the sectors seeing stronger AI adoption. Vallés pointed to Vietnam's Techcombank as an example, saying the bank is using AI to assess loan applications and expand access to credit for small businesses. The technology has helped the bank to analyze more data and approve some loan applications that might otherwise have been rejected, he said. Techcombank, one of Vietnam's largest commercial banks, serves more than 16.5 million retail and corporate customers. According to an AWS case study , its modernization of digital banking infrastructure using AWS improved application response times by up to 35% and cut the time needed to launch new product features by 30%. What's next for Asia? AI adoption continued to expand across Asia-Pacific, with all 10 markets surveyed recording increases from the previous year. Australia led the group with an adoption rate of 61%, followed by Singapore at 59% and South Korea at 58%. Still, businesses face significant obstacles to scaling AI investments. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of respondents as an obstacle to adoption or expansion. Despite those challenges, Vallés expressed optimism about Asia-Pacific's role in AI innovation, pointing to the region's cultural diversity and range of perspectives. "I am convinced that most of the innovation in the fullness of time will come from our region," he said. Vallés added that Asia-Pacific has the ingredients to become a global center for innovation, citing its diversity, talent, startup ecosystem and technology. "APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation," he said. Genie is a technological leader in boom lifts with complementary scissor and telehandler products and adds approximately $2.3 billion USD on a last twelve-month basis to Linamar’s Industrial Segment revenue.
